recentItems.title: Saudi Arabia on Alert as Houthi Missile Threat Raises Questions About Riyadh's Security and Defenses
recentItems.description:
Saudi Prince MBS Rushes To  'BUNKER PALACE' In PANIC As HOUTHIS Rain Missiles Like Hell? 

Houthis Vs Saudi Arabia conflict is spiraling out of control. Iran-backed rebels are raining missiles on the kingdom, targeting critical infrastructure, including Riyadh’s international airport. And now, as the threat intensifies, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is reportedly being moved between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers, amid mounting security fears. The 41-year-old crown prince is reportedly being protected by a handpicked security team, with officials familiar with the matter telling US media network that his movements are being closely guarded.

recentItems.title: Houthi Missile Threat Raises Alarm in Saudi Arabia as Iran's Military Support Comes Under Scrutiny
recentItems.description:
The Houthis are thirsting for vengeance, and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman is staring at lethal missile strikes from the pro-Iran rebels in Yemen.

With a focus on crucial urban centers, the Houthis are zeroing in on airports within the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as well as Dammam, strategically located along the Persian Gulf adjacent to Bahrain and Qatar.

As tensions skyrocket, Saudi Arabia and its allies must stop Houthi resupply.

As per the Council on Foreign Relations, Iran is the Houthis’ primary benefactor, providing them with security assistance, such as weapons transfers, training, and intelligence support.

Such aid typically reaches the Houthis via Iran’s paramilitary Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or the IRGC, which also helps advise the Houthis’ military command.

Iran facilitates a supply of more sophisticated weaponry than the Houthis could acquire on their own, especially missiles and drones.

While Iranian support has helped the Houthis gain and maintain military superiority within Yemen, experts say it has had greater effect elsewhere.

The role of Iran has been decisive in providing the Houthis with smuggled weapons and expertise to project power into the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait.

The Houthis assist Iran by menacing Saudi Arabia’s border and protecting Iranian ships in the Red Sea, giving Iran room to evade sanctions on oil shipping by distracting its enemies and facilitating a shadow network.

At the same time, experts say Yemen offers a testing ground for Iranian weapons on its front lines and in the Red Sea.

Like all Axis of Resistance members in Iran’s proxy network, the Houthis offer Iran plausible deniability: Members routinely claim responsibility for attacks likely ordered or perpetrated by Iran.

recentItems.title: Abu Dhabi Hosts Major Security Summit as Iran-Backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia Face Rising Tensions
recentItems.description:
Abu Dhabi Hosts Major Security Summit as Iran-Backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia Face Rising Tensions

Security experts and officers from 26 countries gathered on Monday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of United Arab Emirates for the 6th annual TRENDS conference.

This year's theme was “the post-war future of the Middle East”.

The conference aimed to address regional transformation, security and stability in the context of the region's ongoing wars.

Dr. Ali Al Nuaimi, a member of the UAE Federal National Council, told the audience that escalating tensions between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia threaten regional and international stability.

“Targeting the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is not only to target the Gulf countries, but it is to target the entire region and to target global security,” he said.

Al Nuaimi added that sustainable security requires political will and new regional order.
